claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in tungsten-based refractory alloys is primarily governed by diffusion-assisted dislocation climb at grain boundaries.
High-temperature toughness in tungsten-based refractory alloys is primarily governed by diffusion-assisted dislocation climb at grain boundaries.
Atomic diffusion along grain boundaries enables dislocation climb at elevated temperatures.
A suitable dopant will segregate to tungsten-alloy grain boundaries.
The segregating dopant can increase grain-boundary cohesion.
Dopant segregation will lower grain-boundary diffusivity.
Lower grain-boundary diffusivity impedes dislocation climb.
Suppressing diffusion-assisted dislocation climb will reduce high-temperature plastic strain rate.
The doped alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength than the undoped baseline.
Reduced dislocation climb may alter strain-hardening behavior.
Reduced dislocation climb may alter toughness by changing the balance between ductility and strength.
The range 600–800 °C represents a diffusion-activated high-temperature regime for the proposed tungsten-based alloys.
High-temperature grain-boundary deformation can play a leading role relative to intragranular dislocation slip.
Keeping grain size, processing, and other microstructural features constant is intended to isolate the effect of grain-boundary chemistry.
The proposed relationship should hold only in a diffusion-activated regime below melting and when microstructural features other than grain-boundary chemistry remain similar.
The magnitude of the response depends on dopant identity and concentration.
The magnitude of the response depends on processing conditions.
Failure to alter grain-boundary chemistry is specified as an outcome that falsifies the mechanistic hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention proposes adding a dopant while keeping bulk composition constant; without a specified substitution or exclusively interfacial delivery method, adding a dopant necessarily changes overall composition.

The samples are said to be tested under identical strain rates, but plastic strain rate is also the principal response to be compared in constant-load or creep testing. In such tests it cannot simultaneously be fixed and treated as the measured outcome.

Failure of the dopant to alter grain-boundary chemistry is labeled as falsification, but it instead represents failure to implement the proposed mediator and therefore does not test whether changed diffusivity would affect climb.
